newsitem.title: USA: FIGURE SKATING-ELDREDGE NURSING LEG AS WORLDS APPROACH.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-ELDREDGE NURSING LEG AS WORLDS APPROACH.

text.p: With just six days to go before Todd Eldredge begins his defence of his world figure skating crown in Lausanne, Switzerland, the four-time national champ is nursing an injured ankle.

"Last Thursday during practice I over-rotated a triple Axel and my right free leg went into the ice really hard, jammed and I sprained my ankle. I'm going to therapy twice a day, getting ultrasound and icing it before and after I skate," Eldredge, 25, said on Monday in a teleconference from his Bloomfield Hills training site 30 miles north of Detroit.

"It started feeling better yesterday," he said Monday, noting he had been able to skate his programme earlier in the morning and missed only one element. "It's tender but I've got 'til Sunday for the qualifying round." (This year all skaters, even the reigning champ, must compete in the qualifier to earn a berth in the actual Championship.)

The injury forced Eldredge off the ice for two days last week and has all but dashed his hopes of adding a quadruple jump to his repertoire at Worlds since the take-off for that daunting jump could put too much pressure on his injured foot.
Ironically, Eldredge said he had landed a quadruple toe loop just seconds before the Axel went awry.

Even before the mishap, however, Eldredge faced an uphill battle in Lausanne following his second place finish at the Champions Series Final 10 days ago. In that event, the Massachusetts-born athlete was held at bay by the sport's technical wizard Elvis Stojko, Canada's 1994 and 1995 world champ, who also made history there by landing the world's first quadruple-triple jump combination.
When arch rivals Alexei Urmanov and Ilia Kulik, of Russia, also nailed their quadruple jumps that left Eldredge with the only quad-free programme among the prime contenders for world gold.

"With the foot the way it is, the quad's not in the programme now. When we get (to Switzerland), we'll think about it but right now I don't see that happening," Eldredge said frankly. "I don't think the quad is a must. If you do it, they'll give you an extra tenth (of a point) on the technical mark but what it comes down to is the most well-rounded programme is going to win."
Although Eldredge remained optimistic that he could win next week he noted, "The sport has changed so much that there's four or five guys that are equally as good and could win it on a given night.
"Elvis skated great (at the Series Final) and if he goes to World's and skates like that, he'll be tough to beat."
Meanwhile, Eldredge's training mate and U.S. women's champion Tara Lipinski, 14, seems to be sailing along without a care in the world after scoring major upsets in her last two outings.

In February she unseated world champion Michelle Kwan for the U.S. title and two weeks later, delivered a carbon copy of that performance for another surprise win over Kwan and three experienced Russian women at the Champions Series Final.
The whirling dervish from Sugar Land, Texas, who finished only 15th at the 1996 Worlds, has little to lose and everything to gain in Lausanne.
"I don't feel much pressure going in," she said. "I can only get better.
"It would be very hard (to win). Anything could happen but everyone's going to be there trying to skate their best," said Lipinski refusing to address her medal potential.
Last fall before she began winning medal after medal on the international circuit, Lipinski stated her long-term goal was to win the Olympics. She didn't say which one.

But her coach Richard Callaghan, who also trains Eldredge, believes Lipinski can win both the 1998 and 2002 Games. For Lipinski, however, merely qualifying for the 1998 Olympic team will be a dream come true.

In addition to Eldredge, Lipinski and Kwan, three other U.S. skaters will compete in the men's and women's events in Lausanne. They are Michael Weiss, 20, Dan Hollander, 24, and '95 national champ Nicole Bobek, 19.
